Evidence:
Goals Against are the number of goals recorded while the goalie is on the ice; the most Goal Againsts refers to MAX(GA); Minnesota North Stars is name of team;
answer: SELECT playerID FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Teams AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T2.name = 'Minnesota North Stars' GROUP BY T1.playerID ORDER BY SUM(T1.GA) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from goalie performance records and link each record to the corresponding team using both the team identifier and season year: `FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Teams AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the joined records to seasons played for the Minnesota North Stars by matching the team name: `WHERE T2.name = 'Minnesota North Stars'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Combine all qualifying season or stint records for each goalkeeper so their Goals Against values can be totaled across their play time: `GROUP BY T1.playerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the goalkeepers from highest to lowest total Goals Against and retain only the top-ranked goalkeeper: `ORDER BY SUM(T1.GA) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the identifier of the goalkeeper who ranks first after aggregation and sorting: `SELECT playerID`.

Question:
What's Lucas di Grassi's Q1 result in the race No. 345?

Evidence:
race number refers to raceId;
answer: SELECT T1.q1 FROM qualifying AS T1 INNER JOIN drivers AS T2 ON T2.driverId = T1.driverId WHERE T1.raceId = 345 AND T2.forename = 'Lucas' AND T2.surname = 'di Grassi'

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the qualifying records to race No. 345, where the race number refers to `raceId`: `WHERE T1.raceId = 345`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Identify Lucas di Grassi by applying conditions to both his forename and surname: `AND T2.forename = 'Lucas' AND T2.surname = 'di Grassi'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the Q1 result from the matching qualifying record in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.q1`.

Question:
Show the ids for all the faculty members who have at least 2 students.
answer: SELECT T1.FacID FROM Faculty AS T1 JOIN Student AS T2 ON T1.FacID  =  T2.advisor GROUP BY T1.FacID HAVING count(*)  >=  2

Question:
How much more expensive in percentage is the product with the highest selling price from the product with the lowest selling price in the Clothing category?

Evidence:
selling price refers to ListPrice; highest selling price refers to MAX(ListPrice); lowest selling price refers to MIN(ListPrice);
answer: SELECT (MAX(T1.ListPrice) - MIN(T1.ListPrice)) * 100 / MIN(T1.ListPrice) FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductSubcategory AS T2 ON T1.ProductSubcategoryID = T2.ProductSubcategoryID INNER JOIN ProductCategory AS T3 ON T2.ProductCategoryID = T3.ProductCategoryID WHERE T3.Name = 'Clothing'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from products, where each item's selling price is stored in `ListPrice`, and link each product to its subcategory: `FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductSubcategory AS T2 ON T1.ProductSubcategoryID = T2.ProductSubcategoryID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Continue from each subcategory to its parent category so the category name can be identified: `INNER JOIN ProductCategory AS T3 ON T2.ProductCategoryID = T3.ProductCategoryID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined product records to those belonging to the Clothing category: `WHERE T3.Name = 'Clothing'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Find the highest and lowest selling prices among the filtered products using the two aggregate expressions: `MAX(T1.ListPrice)` and `MIN(T1.ListPrice)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate how much higher the maximum price is than the minimum as a percentage of the minimum price in the projection: `SELECT (MAX(T1.ListPrice) - MIN(T1.ListPrice)) * 100 / MIN(T1.ListPrice)`.

Question:
From 1980 to 1983, how many of the NBA All-Star players have more than 60% three point rate?

Evidence:
from 1980 to 1983 refers to year BETWEEN 1980 and 1983; NBA refers to lgID = 'NBA'; more than 60% three point rate refers to divide(threeMade, threeAttempted) > 0.6
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T2.playerID FROM player_allstar AS T1 INNER JOIN players_teams AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T2.year BETWEEN 1980 AND 1983 AND T1.three_made / T1.three_attempted > 0.6

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the All-Star appearance records, which contain each player’s three-point makes and attempts: `FROM player_allstar AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each All-Star to the player-team records by the shared player identifier so the relevant team season year is available: `INNER JOIN players_teams AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the player-team seasons to the inclusive period from 1980 through 1983: `WHERE T2.year BETWEEN 1980 AND 1983`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep All-Star records whose three-point makes divided by attempts produce a rate greater than 60 percent: `AND T1.three_made / T1.three_attempted > 0.6`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project each qualifying player identifier once, using DISTINCT to remove duplicates caused by multiple season or team records: `SELECT DISTINCT T2.playerID`.

Question:
Calculate the percentage whereby Hamilton was not at the 1st track of the the f1 circuit since 2010.

Evidence:
percentage = DIVIDE(COUNT(raceId) where surname = 'Hamilton' and position>1), (COUNT(raceId) where surname = 'Hamilton'); since 2010 refers to year >= 2010
answer: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T2.position <> 1 THEN T2.position END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T2.driverStandingsId) FROM races AS T1 INNER JOIN driverStandings AS T2 ON T2.raceId = T1.raceId INNER JOIN drivers AS T3 ON T3.driverId = T2.driverId WHERE T3.surname = 'Hamilton' AND T1.year >= 2010

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from races and connect each race to its driver standings using the shared race identifier: `FROM races AS T1 INNER JOIN driverStandings AS T2 ON T2.raceId = T1.raceId`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the standings to driver details so Hamilton can be identified by surname: `INNER JOIN drivers AS T3 ON T3.driverId = T2.driverId`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the records to Hamilton's standings from the 2010 season onward: `WHERE T3.surname = 'Hamilton' AND T1.year >= 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Count Hamilton's standings where his position was not first by conditionally retaining non-first positions: `COUNT(CASE WHEN T2.position <> 1 THEN T2.position END)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the percentage by casting the conditional count to REAL, multiplying by 100, and dividing by all matching standings records: `SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T2.position <> 1 THEN T2.position END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T2.driverStandingsId)`.

Question:
From 1950 to 1970, how many coaches who received more than 1 award?

Evidence:
from 1950 to 1970 refers to year between 1950 and 1970; more than 3 awards refers to count(award) > 3
answer: SELECT COUNT(coachID) FROM awards_coaches WHERE year BETWEEN 1950 AND 1970 GROUP BY coachID HAVING COUNT(coachID) > 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the table containing coach award records, since it provides the coach identifier, award, and year: `FROM awards_coaches`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the award records to the inclusive period from 1950 through 1970: `WHERE year BETWEEN 1950 AND 1970`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the filtered award records by coach so each coach's awards can be counted separately: `GROUP BY coachID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only coach groups containing more than one award record: `HAVING COUNT(coachID) > 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the count of award records for each qualifying coach in the SELECT clause: `SELECT COUNT(coachID)`.

Question:

average number of papers refers to DIVIDE(count(id), 9); published from 2002 to 2010 refers to Year BETWEEN 2002 AND 2010; 'Information and Knowledge Engineering' is the FullName of conference;

Question:
Which position has won the most awards and who is the most recent player that was awarded with an award in that position? Indicate the name of the award and the full name of the player.

Evidence:
position has won the most awards refers to pos(max(count(award))); most recent player refers to playerID(pos(max(count(award)))& max(year)); full name = nameGiven + lastName
answer: SELECT T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN AwardsCoaches AS T2 ON T2.coachID = T1.coachID GROUP BY T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName ORDER BY COUNT(T2.award) LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with player and coach identity information from `Master`, assigning the alias used for its position and name columns: `FROM Master AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each master record to its coach awards through the shared coach identifier: `INNER JOIN AwardsCoaches AS T2 ON T2.coachID = T1.coachID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create groups for every distinct combination of position, award, and player name so the awards can be counted: `GROUP BY T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the grouped results by their award count and retain the first result: `ORDER BY COUNT(T2.award) LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the position, award name, and the two components of the player's full name in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict expenses to those dated from September 10, 2019 through November 19, 2019, inclusively: `WHERE date(SUBSTR(T2.expense_date, 1, 10)) BETWEEN '2019-09-10' AND '2019-11-19'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Further restrict the qualifying expenses to payments costing more than 20 dollars: `AND T2.cost > 20`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the members' email addresses and deduplicate people who have multiple qualifying expenses: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.email`.

Question:
What is the credit rating of the company whose average lead time is 16 days for a standard price of 18.9900 and whose last receipt date is August 27, 2011?

Evidence:
last receipt date is August 17, 2011 refers to LastReceiptDate> = '2011-08-17 00:00:00' and LastReceiptDate < '2011-08-18 00:00:00';
answer: SELECT T2.CreditRating FROM ProductVendor AS T1 INNER JOIN Vendor AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.StandardPrice = 18.9900 AND T1.AverageLeadTime = 16 AND STRFTIME('%Y-%m-%d', T1.LastReceiptDate) = '2011-08-27'

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the records to the specified standard price and average lead time: `WHERE T1.StandardPrice = 18.9900 AND T1.AverageLeadTime = 16`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the receipt-date condition by extracting the date portion and matching August 27, 2011: `AND STRFTIME('%Y-%m-%d', T1.LastReceiptDate) = '2011-08-27'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the credit rating from the matching vendor record in the projection: `SELECT T2.CreditRating`.

Question:

Evidence:

Question:
Which different vendor has the most amount of orders? Calculate the total estimated earnings.

Evidence:
amount of order refers to quantityOrdered; most amount of orders refers to SUM(QuantityOrdered); estimated earnings refers to expected profits; expected profits = SUBTRACT(msrp, buyPrice);
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.productVendor, T1.MSRP - T1.buyPrice FROM products AS T1 INNER JOIN orderdetails AS T2 ON T1.productCode = T2.productCode GROUP BY T1.productVendor, T1.MSRP, T1.buyPrice ORDER BY COUNT(T2.quantityOrdered) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each product to its order-detail records through the shared product code so vendor and pricing data can be analyzed alongside ordered quantities: `FROM products AS T1 INNER JOIN orderdetails AS T2 ON T1.productCode = T2.productCode`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined records by vendor and the two price fields needed for the earnings calculation: `GROUP BY T1.productVendor, T1.MSRP, T1.buyPrice`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Rank the groups by the count of ordered-quantity records in descending order, then retain the top result: `ORDER BY COUNT(T2.quantityOrdered) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Calculate estimated earnings as the difference between the manufacturer's suggested retail price and the product's buy price: `T1.MSRP - T1.buyPrice`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the distinct vendor together with the estimated-earnings expression before the join, grouping, and ranking clauses: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.productVendor, T1.MSRP - T1.buyPrice`.

which load shape has the highest number refers to MAX(load_shape); head car refers to position = 1; east is a direction; calculation = MULTIPLY(DIVIDE(count(direction = 'east' where MAX(load_shape) where position = 1 then id), count(id)), 100)
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T3.load_shape FROM ( SELECT load_shape, train_id FROM cars WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY train_id DESC ) AS T3 UNION ALL SELECT T4.load_shape FROM ( SELECT load_shape, train_id FROM cars WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY train_id DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS T4 UNION ALL SELECT (CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN T2.direction = 'east' THEN T2.id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(DISTINCT T2.id)) FROM cars AS T1 INNER JOIN trains AS T2 ON T1.train_id = T2.id WHERE T1.position = 1 AND T1.load_shape = ( SELECT T4.load_shape FROM ( SELECT load_shape, train_id FROM cars AS T WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY train_id DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS T4 )

prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the percentage by conditionally counting distinct eastbound train IDs, casting that count to REAL, and dividing by all distinct qualifying train IDs; combine the three result sections in order with `UNION ALL`: `SELECT (CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN T2.direction = 'east' THEN T2.id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(DISTINCT T2.id))` and `UNION ALL`.

Question:
How many products that take more than 2 days to make are out of stock?

Evidence:
take more than 2 days to make refers to DaysToManufacture>2; out of stock refers to OnOrderQty = 0 or OnOrderQty is null

Question:
Identify the customer, which placed the largest order in terms of value.

Evidence:
value refers to SUM(UnitPrice * Quantity * SUBTRACT(1, Discount)); the largest order in value refers to MAX(value)
answer: SELECT T1.CompanyName FROM Customers AS T1 INNER JOIN Orders AS T2 ON T1.CustomerID = T2.CustomerID INNER JOIN `Order Details` AS T3 ON T2.OrderID = T3.OrderID GROUP BY T2.CustomerID ORDER BY SUM(T3.UnitPrice * T3.Quantity * (1 - T3.Discount)) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_3: Combine the joined rows by customer so the line-item values can be aggregated for each customer: `GROUP BY T2.CustomerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank customers by the sum of discounted line-item values and retain the one with the greatest total: `ORDER BY SUM(T3.UnitPrice * T3.Quantity * (1 - T3.Discount)) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the company name of the highest-ranked customer by placing this clause at the beginning of the assembled query: `SELECT T1.CompanyName`.

Question:
Among the coaches who taught the teams in 1922's Stanley Cup finals, how many of them are from the USA?

Evidence:
from the USA refers to birthCountry = 'USA'; year = 1922;
answer: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T3.coachID) FROM Coaches AS T1 INNER JOIN TeamsSC AS T2 ON T1.year = T2.year AND T1.tmID = T2.tmID INNER JOIN Master AS T3 ON T1.coachID = T3.coachID WHERE T2.year = 1922 AND T3.birthCountry = 'USA'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the coaches and connect them to Stanley Cup team records using both the season and team identifiers: `FROM Coaches AS T1 INNER JOIN TeamsSC AS T2 ON T1.year = T2.year AND T1.tmID = T2.tmID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each coach to the biographical information in `Master` through the shared coach identifier: `INNER JOIN Master AS T3 ON T1.coachID = T3.coachID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the Stanley Cup team records to the specified 1922 season: `WHERE T2.year = 1922`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the nationality condition so only coaches whose recorded birth country is the USA qualify: `AND T3.birthCountry = 'USA'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count distinct coach identifiers so each qualifying coach is counted once even if multiple matching records exist: `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T3.coachID)`.

Question:
How many products from the Clothing category were on the LL Road Frame Sale?

Evidence:
LL Road Frame Sale is a description of special offer
answer: SELECT COUNT(T2.ProductID) FROM SpecialOffer AS T1 INNER JOIN SpecialOfferProduct AS T2 ON T1.SpecialOfferID = T2.SpecialOfferID INNER JOIN Product AS T3 ON T2.ProductID = T3.ProductID INNER JOIN ProductSubcategory AS T4 ON T3.ProductSubcategoryID = T4.ProductSubcategoryID INNER JOIN ProductCategory AS T5 ON T4.ProductCategoryID = T5.ProductCategoryID WHERE T1.Description = 'LL Road Frame Sale' AND T4.Name = 'Clothing'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the special-offer table and connect the named offer to its associated products through the shared offer identifier: `FROM SpecialOffer AS T1 INNER JOIN SpecialOfferProduct AS T2 ON T1.SpecialOfferID = T2.SpecialOfferID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each offer-product record to the corresponding product so its classification can be followed: `INNER JOIN Product AS T3 ON T2.ProductID = T3.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Continue through the product hierarchy by joining each product to its subcategory: `INNER JOIN ProductSubcategory AS T4 ON T3.ProductSubcategoryID = T4.ProductSubcategoryID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Connect the subcategory to its parent category, then restrict the rows to the specified offer description and Clothing name: `INNER JOIN ProductCategory AS T5 ON T4.ProductCategoryID = T5.ProductCategoryID WHERE T1.Description = 'LL Road Frame Sale' AND T4.Name = 'Clothing'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the product identifiers remaining after the joins and filters by using this projection at the beginning of the query: `SELECT COUNT(T2.ProductID)`.

Question:
Give the cohort name for the school with biggest cohort size.

Evidence:
biggest cohort size refers to MAX(cohort_size); cohort = '4y bach' means bachelor's or equivalent-seeking cohort at 4-year institutions; cohort = '4y other' means students seeking another type of degree or certificate at a 4-year institution; cohort = '2y all' means degree-seeking students at 2-year institutions;
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.chronname FROM institution_details AS T1 INNER JOIN institution_grads AS T2 ON T2.unitid = T1.unitid WHERE T1.cohort_size = ( SELECT MAX(T1.cohort_size) FROM institution_details AS T1 INNER JOIN institution_grads AS T2 ON T2.unitid = T1.unitid )

prefix_hints.hint_1: Determine the largest recorded cohort size using the aggregate expression `MAX(T1.cohort_size)`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Build a scalar subquery over institutions joined to their graduation records so it returns that maximum size: `( SELECT MAX(T1.cohort_size) FROM institution_details AS T1 INNER JOIN institution_grads AS T2 ON T2.unitid = T1.unitid )`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: For the outer query, connect each institution to its graduation records through the shared institution identifier: `FROM institution_details AS T1 INNER JOIN institution_grads AS T2 ON T2.unitid = T1.unitid`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only institutions whose cohort size equals the maximum calculated by the scalar subquery: `WHERE T1.cohort_size = ( SELECT MAX(T1.cohort_size) FROM institution_details AS T1 INNER JOIN institution_grads AS T2 ON T2.unitid = T1.unitid )`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return each qualifying school name once, since the graduation join can produce multiple rows per institution: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.chronname`.

Question:
How long does it take for the business to receive the item it has purchased? Who is the vendor for business number 1496?

Evidence:
business number refers to BusinessEntityID where BusinessEntityID = 1496; how long does it take refers to AverageLeadTime
answer: SELECT T1.AverageLeadTime, T2.Name FROM ProductVendor AS T1 INNER JOIN Vendor AS T2 USING (businessentityid) WHERE T2.BusinessEntityID = 1496 GROUP BY T1.AverageLeadTime, T2.Name

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use `ProductVendor` as the source of the requested purchasing lead time, assigning the target alias: `FROM ProductVendor AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the vendor records so each product-vendor entry is associated with its vendor name through the shared business entity identifier: `INNER JOIN Vendor AS T2 USING (businessentityid)`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to business number 1496 using the vendor's identifier: `WHERE T2.BusinessEntityID = 1496`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Group identical lead-time and vendor-name combinations so repeated product-vendor records produce distinct result combinations: `GROUP BY T1.AverageLeadTime, T2.Name`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested average lead time and vendor name from their respective aliases: `SELECT T1.AverageLeadTime, T2.Name`.

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each salary record to the corresponding player and team so that player names and the team name are available: `FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Build the first result set by restricting salary records to the Washington Nationals in 2005: `WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Project the first and last names for the players qualifying in the 2005 result set: `SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Construct the parallel result set for players paid by the same team in 2007, using the identical joins and name projection: `SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2007 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Keep only names appearing in both yearly result sets by placing the set-intersection operator between the completed 2005 branch and the 2007 branch: `INTERSECT`.

answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(T1.VacationHours) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.PersonType = 'SP'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from `Employee`, which contains both vacation hours and the employee business entity identifier: `FROM Employee AS T1`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Build the average from the total vacation hours divided by the number of qualifying employees: `SUM(T1.VacationHours) / COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID)`.

Question:
What is the full name of the Vice President of Production?

Evidence:
full name = FirstName+MiddleName+LastName; Vice President of Production is a JobTitle;
answer: SELECT T2.FirstName, T2.MiddleName, T2.LastName FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle = 'Vice President of Production'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the employee records because `JobTitle` identifies the role being requested: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each employee to the corresponding person record using the shared business entity identifier: `INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Identify the exact job-title comparison that selects the Vice President of Production: `T1.JobTitle = 'Vice President of Production'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Apply that comparison as the row filter after the joined tables: `WHERE T1.JobTitle = 'Vice President of Production'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the three name components from the matched `Person` record to provide the full name: `SELECT T2.FirstName, T2.MiddleName, T2.LastName`.

answer: SELECT T2.PlayerName, T1.height_in_cm FROM height_info AS T1 INNER JOIN PlayerInfo AS T2 ON T1.height_id = T2.height WHERE T2.height = ( SELECT height FROM PlayerInfo WHERE PlayerName = 'Brian Gionta' )

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the laboratory records to the two RA values representing a normal Rheumatoid Factor result: `WHERE (T2.RA = '-' OR T2.RA = '+-')`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the birthday condition so that only patients born after January 1, 1985 qualify: `AND T1.Birthday > '1985-01-01'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the disease recorded in the patient diagnosis column by placing this clause at the beginning of the assembled query: `SELECT T1.Diagnosis`.

Question:
How many employees in the Information Service department work the evening shift?

Evidence:
Information Service is a name of department;
answer: SELECT COUNT(T2.BusinessEntityID) FROM Department AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.DepartmentID = T2.DepartmentID INNER JOIN Shift AS T3 ON T2.ShiftId = T3.ShiftId WHERE T1.Name = 'Information Services' AND T3.Name = 'Evening'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the department table and connect each department to its employee assignment history using the shared department identifier: `FROM Department AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.DepartmentID = T2.DepartmentID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Extend the joined data to the shift table so each employee assignment can be matched to its shift name: `INNER JOIN Shift AS T3 ON T2.ShiftId = T3.ShiftId`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the assignments to the department whose stored name is Information Services: `WHERE T1.Name = 'Information Services'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the shift-name condition so only evening-shift assignments remain: `AND T3.Name = 'Evening'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the employee identifiers among the qualifying assignment rows in the projection: `SELECT COUNT(T2.BusinessEntityID)`.

Question:
Find the country of all appelations who have at most three wines.
answer: SELECT T1.County FROM APPELLATIONS AS T1 JOIN WINE AS T2 ON T1.Appelation  =  T2.Appelation GROUP BY T2.Appelation HAVING count(*)  <=  3

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the `WINE` table as the source of individual wine records and assign it the target alias: `WINE AS T2`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each wine to its appellation record so its county can be retrieved: `FROM APPELLATIONS AS T1 JOIN WINE AS T2 ON T1.Appelation = T2.Appelation`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined wine records by appellation so the wines belonging to each appellation can be counted: `GROUP BY T2.Appelation`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only appellation groups containing at most three wine records: `HAVING count(*) <= 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the county associated with each qualifying appellation using the outer SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.County`.

Question:
Among the employees who have more than 10 hours of sick leave, how many of them wish to receive e-mail promotions?

Evidence:
Contact does wish to receive e-mail promotions refers to EmailPromotion = (1,2); more than 10 hours of sick leave refer to SickLeaveHours >10;
answer: SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.EmailPromotion = 1 AND T1.SickLeaveHours > 10

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the employee records because `SickLeaveHours` and the employee identifier are stored there: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each employee to their person record so the e-mail promotion preference is available: `INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to people whose e-mail promotion preference has the qualifying value 1: `WHERE T2.EmailPromotion = 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Further restrict the employees to those with more than 10 sick-leave hours: `AND T1.SickLeaveHours > 10`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the business entity identifiers of employees satisfying both conditions in the projection: `SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID)`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the draw-result condition, since `FTR = 'D'` represents matches where both teams scored equal goals: `AND T1.FTR = 'D'`.

Question:
Which dogs are owned by someone who lives in Virginia? List the owner's first name and the dog's name.
answer: SELECT T1.first_name ,  T2.name FROM Owners AS T1 JOIN Dogs AS T2 ON T1.owner_id  =  T2.owner_id WHERE T1.state  =  'Virginia'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the `Owners` table because it contains both the owner’s first name and state, assigning it the target alias: `FROM Owners AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each owner to their dogs through the shared `owner_id` key: `JOIN Dogs AS T2 ON T1.owner_id = T2.owner_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to owners whose state is Virginia: `WHERE T1.state = 'Virginia'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Identify the two requested output columns: the owner’s first name is `T1.first_name`, and the dog’s name is `T2.name`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project those columns at the beginning of the assembled join-and-filter query: `SELECT T1.first_name, T2.name`.

answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(IIF(T2.n_name = 'IRAN', 1, 0)) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T2.n_name) FROM customer AS T1 INNER JOIN nation AS T2 ON T1.c_nationkey = T2.n_nationkey WHERE T1.c_mktsegment = 'HOUSEHOLD'

Question:
Among the orders shipped in November, 1998 by air, how many orders were urgent?

orders shipped in November, 1998 refer to o_orderkey where l_shipdate LIKE '1998-11-%'; by air refers to l_shipmode = 'AIR'; the order is urgent if o_orderpriority = '1-URGENT' ;
answer: SELECT COUNT(T1.o_orderkey) FROM orders AS T1 INNER JOIN lineitem AS T2 ON T1.o_orderkey = T2.l_orderkey WHERE T2.l_shipmode = 'AIR' AND T1.o_orderpriority = '1-URGENT' AND SUBSTR(T2.l_shipdate, 1, 7) = '1998-11'

prefix_hints.hint_3: Identify urgent orders by adding the exact order-priority condition: `AND T1.o_orderpriority = '1-URGENT'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Limit shipments to November 1998 by extracting the year-month portion of the shipping date: `AND SUBSTR(T2.l_shipdate, 1, 7) = '1998-11'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the order keys remaining after the join and all shipment and priority filters: `SELECT COUNT(T1.o_orderkey)`.

Question:
For the goalie who had the highest defensive success rate in the postseason of 2011, what's his legends ID ?

Evidence:
Post season of 2011 refers to year = ’2011’
defensive success rate refers to (SUBTRACT(1 (DIVIDE(PostGA/PostSA)), *100%)
answer: SELECT T2.legendsID FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.year = 2011 ORDER BY 1 - CAST(T1.PostGA AS REAL) / T1.PostSA DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the goalie statistics table, which contains the postseason goals allowed and shots against needed to measure defensive success: `FROM Goalies AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each goalie record to the player master data so the corresponding legends ID can be retrieved: `INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the goalie records to the 2011 season as specified: `WHERE T1.year = 2011`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank goalies from highest to lowest defensive success rate; casting `PostGA` to REAL ensures decimal division, while multiplying by 100 is unnecessary for ranking: `ORDER BY 1 - CAST(T1.PostGA AS REAL) / T1.PostSA DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the legends ID and retain only the top-ranked goalie using these final clauses: `SELECT T2.legendsID` and `LIMIT 1`.

Question:
how long is the longest river in texas
answer: SELECT LENGTH FROM river WHERE LENGTH  =  ( SELECT MAX ( LENGTH ) FROM river WHERE traverse  =  "texas" ) AND traverse  =  "texas";

prefix_hints.hint_3: Use `river` as the outer query’s source so the matching length can be returned: `FROM river`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Match the outer river to the calculated maximum and ensure it also traverses Texas: `WHERE LENGTH = ( SELECT MAX ( LENGTH ) FROM river WHERE traverse = "texas" ) AND traverse = "texas"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the length of the qualifying longest river in the outer query: `SELECT LENGTH`.
